newsitem.title: MOLDOVA: Former Kremlin insider wins Moldovan presidency.
newsitem.headline: Former Kremlin insider wins Moldovan presidency.

text.p: Petru Lucinschi, who was once a leading communist official in the Kremlin, was elected president of Moldova after beating the former Soviet republic's first post-independence leader in a run-off vote on Sunday.

Preliminary results on Monday gave the 56-year-old chairman of the national parliament an eight-point win over President Mircea Snegur, with 54 percent to 46 percent. Turnout was 72 percent compared to 67 percent in the November 17 first round.

Lucinschi, who was secretary of the Communist Party central committee in the final days of the Soviet Union, presents himself as a social democrat in the mould of other east European ex-communists who have won back power through elections.
Favouring good relations with Moscow, he attacked as "savage capitalism" Snegur's plans for faster market reforms, such as the complete privatisation of rural Moldova's land.

Backed by much of the media, Lucinschi also played on the one-third Russian-speaking minority's fears of the president's call for closer ties to Romania, from whose territory and people Stalin carved most of the republic in 1940.

At his first news conference on Monday, the president-elect said he would use his influence in the Kremlin to secure fuel for the winter -- Moldova is deeply in debt to Russian energy suppliers -- and also to settle other outstanding issues.
"I will use my ties in Moscow for the good of the country," he said, while stressing he also wanted good relations with the West. He agrees with Snegur's opposition to joining NATO.
"We will continue integration in Europe, but will also strengthen traditional ties with our good neighbours -- Ukraine and Russia," the tall, bespectacled intellectual said.

He plans to finalise an accord, brokered by Moscow, to re- integrate the 700,000-strong Russian-speaking Dnestr region, which broke away in 1990 over fears of Romanian domination, and to repatriate the 6,000 Russian troops who have kept the peace there since fighting in 1992 in which hundreds of people died.
The speaker of Dnestr's parliament welcomed Lucinschi's election as a promising sign for talks on improving relations.

A historian by training, Lucinschi advocates gradual economic reform, making use of international assistance and with a heavy dose of welfare guarantees to ease the pain of change for the impoverished rural nation of 4.3 million.

Snegur, 56, accepted defeat but issued a statement saying he would continue to fight "attempts to restore communism". He was due to speak in Lisbon on Tuesday at the summit of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).
Lucinschi's four-year term will begin only on January 15.
Electoral officials noted no major violations of voting rules. Foreign observers from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe also had no reports of serious trouble.
Moldovans hurrying to work on a wet Monday morning in the city centre took the news of change with a note of fatalism.
"I voted for Snegur," said Svetlana, a 27-year-old philologist. "But really, I don't think it makes a difference."
Valentina, who lives on a 90 lei ($18) pension, had voted for Lucinschi. "Now I hope he raises my pension and makes sure I get it every month, that's the main thing," she said.
Valeriu, a 40-year-old teacher, said: "What we need is someone really fresh, with new ideas to solve our problems."
"Lucinschi isn't really new," he added. "But perhaps he'll bring some new people into the government, a new generation."
Prime Minister Andrei Sangheli, who backed Lucinschi after being knocked out in the first round, repeated he would resign.
Lucinschi said he would form a coalition that could include liberals, social democrats and communists.
